signals.title: Neo4j releases Relate, an open source in-memory database built for AI agents
signals.excerpt:
- Relate is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and built in Rust

...

One caveat up front: the article is based on a company release, distributed through Business Wire. The performance figures are the vendor's own, and the source gives no independent benchmarks or pricing details.

...

Another choice limits how much comes back. Relate caps the number of rows in a result and adds a marker showing the result was cut short. The point is to avoid overfilling an agent's context window, the limited amount of text a model can consider at once.

...

Connectivity comes built in. Relate has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a common standard for letting agents use outside tools, plus a command-line tool. It also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints, so existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks and developer tools should work with it.

## Graph queries and retrieval

Relate supports Cypher, the query language Neo4j uses for graph data. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity, which finds items with similar meaning, and follow connections through the graph in the same step. Neo4j says this supports multi-hop reasoning, where an answer depends on following several links in a row, and GraphRAG, which feeds a model facts drawn from a graph. The company says this gives agents more accurate results and fewer hallucinations, meaning invented answers. That claim is Neo4j's and is not tested in the source.

The release says Relate is 100% openCypher compliant and more than 97% compliant with GQL, the standard graph query language. Those numbers suggest queries written for other graph systems may carry over, though the source does not say how that was measured. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, a permissive open source license.

signals.title: Hugging Face describes CQ quantization and GCMP adapters · Tensor Journal
signals.excerpt:
Hugging Face says it describes CQ, a calibration-free quantization format, and GCMP, a parameter-efficient adapter positioned as a replacement for LoRA. The material is dated November 14, 2026.

Hugging Face says CQ needs no calibration data. Its input is a Hugging Face checkpoint, and it runs layer by layer. The post says GCMP is compatible with CQ, NF4 and full-precision bases.

Hugging Face lists the CQ model at 18 GB and the NF4 model at 22.4 GB.

The benchmark model is Qwen3.8-27B. In company-reported results, the CQ base scores 0.65 on GSM8K. Hugging Face says CQ shows no significant difference from BF16 across all benchmarks. It reports an NF4 loss of 12.0 points on GSM8K against BF16. Hugging Face gives the benchmark size as 200–1,140 questions per task.

The post reports mean KL divergence on WikiText-2 of 0.0282 for CQ against BF16, and 0.033 for NF4 against BF16.

On Qwen3.8-27B, GCMP has 2.9M parameters, and its adapter is about 11 MB on disk. LoRA at rank thirty-two has about 159M trainable parameters and occupies about 320 MB on disk.

The adapter runs used the Alpaca dataset and a fixed set of training settings, covering steps, batch size, sequence length, learning rate and random seed. Hugging Face says those settings were identical across the compared runs.

Hugging Face reports that, on an NF4 base, GCMP scored 4.0 points higher on GSM8K (p = 0.04) than LoRA.

On ARC-Challenge, Hugging Face reports that CQ with GCMP was lower on ARC-Challenge (−4.2, p = 0.001) than NF4 with GCMP.

Hugging Face says the CQ + LoRA run is still in progress. The first CQ + LoRA adapter it evaluated came from an older trainer version, which the post describes as broken.

Hugging Face reports that CQ trainer step time fell from 27.6 seconds per step before a recent improvement to 8.6 seconds now.

Hugging Face says vLLM serving of GCMP currently requires a CQ base, while GCMP adapters on full-precision models run in Transformers for now. CQ supports pipeline parallelism across GPUs, but tensor parallelism is not yet supported. The post gives a per-token adapter routing buffer in vLLM of ~1 MB.

The CUDA kernels ship compiled.

signals.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
signals.excerpt:
Published 11/16/2026

# Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads

What the harness and the inference engine each have to get right so a long agent session stays fast for long horizon tasks.

- Authors Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)

...

Summary

Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps.

Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more.

This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache.

We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike!

...

## Cache is king

The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one.

Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part.

The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length.

The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again.

Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule.

The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness.

## The harnesses and APIs

On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the `ollama launch` command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows.

Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring.

...

### Keeping the cache alive between turns

...

An agent will often make a tool call and then wait a couple of minutes while tests run. ... So we can also offload the cache to CPU memory while the session is idle and restore it for the next turn.

...

We can't know ahead of time whether a response will be 30 tokens or 30,000, so instead of reserving room for the worst case max ... And we rebuild the running batch on every pass (continuous batching), so when an agent fires off five subagents at once, each new request takes a slot the moment one frees up instead of waiting for the slowest one in a batch to finish.

The upshot for anyone building a harness is that headroom for cache memory, not compute, is usually what limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once. Every oversized tool result, and every subagent carrying irrelevant history takes memory that another session's cache could have used.

signals.title: New Research Challenges GPU Utilization as Measure of Inference Infrastructure
signals.excerpt:
Nov 16, 2026, 09:00 ET

New NAND Research report underscores that busy GPUs aren't an accurate measure of productive output; introduces new Inference Economics Scorecard to measure inference infrastructure by the useful work it delivers, as applied in an eight-hour benchmark with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs and WEKA NeuralMesh.

CHICAGO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From Supercomputing 2026: WEKA, the AI data and memory infrastructure company, in collaboration with market intelligence firm NAND Research, today introduced the Inference Economics Scorecard, a new common framework for measuring inference infrastructure productivity and economic value by the useful work it delivers rather than by how busy it keeps GPUs. The scorecard defines nine measures, including tokens per watt, cost per inference, and context retention. It sets four testing rules, including runs of at least eight hours and counting only successful output. Already applied in a benchmark with Nebius, the AI cloud company, it comes as inference is claiming a growing share of AI infrastructure spending and buyers hit power, memory, and rack-space limits.

...

Why GPU Utilization Falls Short for Inference

For years, training was the dominant AI workload. Because training keeps GPUs busy with large, predictable jobs, GPU utilization became the default measure of AI infrastructure productivity. Inference, especially agentic inference, places very different demands on GPUs. An agent does not simply answer a prompt; it completes a task over many steps, and at each step it re-reads the context it built earlier. After the GPU evicts that context from memory to make room for other users and sessions, it must recompute it when the task returns, and the task makes no further progress until that work is done. The result is a GPU that is fully utilized but unproductive because it wastes cycles recomputing the same tokens multiple times.

The Inference Economics Scorecard measures inference systems at production scale: completed requests across many concurrent users, sustained over hours rather than minutes.

...

From Busy to Productive: How the Scorecard Works The Inference Economics Scorecard defines nine measures of inference performance and economics: tokens per watt, tokens per rack, cost per inference, GPU goodput, time to first token and end-to-end latency, memory efficiency, operational density, agent concurrency, and context retention. It also sets the discipline for testing against them:

- The same workload and service targets across every system tested
- Measurement of the whole serving stack
- Runs of at least eight hours
- Only successful output counted

...

Putting It to the Test: Real Agent Load, Sustained for Eight Hours WEKA and Nebius recently applied the scorecard's rules in a joint benchmark on NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and reported results on several measures. The test ran on one eight-GPU node serving DeepSeek-V4-Pro to 512 active sessions drawn from a corpus of more than 5,000 real agentic coding sessions over eight hours per configuration, counting every failed and timed-out request.

Using WEKA NeuralMesh with Augmented Memory Grid, which pools NVMe across the cluster as a shared context tier, the node produced 3.7x the output tokens per GPU-hour compared with HBM-only serving on the same GPUs, and 97% of successfully completed requests reached a first token within five seconds, up from 44%. On HBM-only serving, 60% of prefill work was recomputed from context the cluster had already processed earlier in the session; with Augmented Memory Grid, 6.8%. At the measured rate, the HBM-only node would need about 30 hours to produce what Augmented Memory Grid produced in eight. The full benchmark is published at weka.io and nebius.com blogs.

...

Reproducible by Design: Open Traces and Tooling The traces and tooling behind the benchmark are open-sourced so anyone can run the same workload on their own systems and compare results on equal terms. Because the traces come from real agentic coding sessions rather than synthetic load, and include the varied timing and complexity of real work, they give any team a realistic stand-in for production.

signals.title: Build a production-grade RAG Agent: Part 2 - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Posted on Nov 16 • Edited on Nov 16 

# Build a production-grade RAG Agent: Part 2 

Let's build the agent and its tools, in TypeScript with the Vercel AI SDK. The ideas carry over to any language or framework, such as Python with Pydantic AI.

The repo has two folders that run on their own and meet only over HTTP: `harness/`, the measure from Part 1, and `agent/`, which you build here. Its README covers the rest.

This is Part 2 of a two-part series:

- Part 1 - The evals. Measuring and deciding what "good" means.
- Part 2 - The agent: tools, the loop, one change at a time

TL;DR

In Part 2, we build the agent: one model, three tools over a library of tax Acts, and a loop. By the end, we have an agent that beats the first iteration (0.582 → 0.729, with confidently wrong answers down from 5 to 0), and a way to spot a real improvement.

## Why an agent, and not one search? 

In my main build, the bigger project this tutorial comes from, I first tested which part of the job matters more: finding the law, or reasoning over it. Each version is compared with the floor, one model call with no tools. The repo doesn't include the first two.

| Version | Against the floor | Questions won / lost / tied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perfect passages: the gold's own sources handed to the model | +0.006: a tie | 27 / 28 / 3 |
| One fixed search: the question searched once, the top passages handed to the model | −0.080 | 17 / 34 / 7 |
| The agent, searching and reading for itself | +0.082 | 34 / 16 / 8 |

Handing over the right sources didn't beat the model's own memory, and one search made it worse. Only the agent, searching and reading for itself, beat the floor.

...

## The library: SQLite, seeded 

The repo ships the three Acts as files in `agent/data/law/`, and a ready-made SQLite library built from them. Copy it in before you start the agent: 

```
npm run seed                 # copies the ready-made library: 5,694 passages and their vectors
npm run seed -- --fresh      # downloads the Acts again and embeds every passage: about a minute and $0.20
npm run fetch-law -- <year>/<number>   # fetches another Act from legislation.govt.nz; then npm run seed -- --fresh

```

SQLite's full-text index is searched by default. Set `EMBEDDINGS=auto` to search by meaning instead: each search then embeds its query first.

...

## Step 3. Tool design 

Next, tools. They let the agent search and read the law, the "retrieval" in RAG, so it answers from sources instead of memory.

> Design tools like APIs: one job each, with a clear set of arguments. Keep the number of tools low and each one simple.
> 
> Tool result = data for model; Tool failure = response for the model to act on

A tool essentially looks like this: 

```
// agent/src/tools/index.ts, trimmed
passage_search: tool({
  description: "What the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns",
  inputSchema: "The arguments the model can call it with",
  execute: (input) => call(() => searchPassages(library, book, input)),
}),

```

The description is the tool's manual: the model reads it every time.

The repo has these tools:

- `library_search`: finds an Act by its title or by what it covers. Nothing it returns can be cited.
- `passage_search`: searches inside the Acts by a query, exact words or a section code, and returns the first 300 characters of each hit. Nothing here can be cited either.
- `library_read`: reads a whole section, or an Act's outline. Only what it returns can be cited, as `[extract:L1]`.
- Optional, with `TOOLS=library,web`: `web_search` and `web_read`, for law and official guidance the library lacks. Web search needs a Firecrawl key.

The first three are the default, and all the agent needs.

## Step 4. The Research Agent 

Now the agent itself. It reasons about the question, calls tools, reads what they return, and answers once it has enough. This is a ReAct agent, named after the 2022 paper ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.

We build this by using the SDK's `generateText`: 

```
// agent/src/agent.ts, trimmed: the floor's call, with tools and a way to stop
const result = await generateText({
  model,
  instructions: instructionsFor(names, today),
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: questionMessage(question, country) }],
  tools,                                                   // library_search, passage_search, library_read
  stopWhen: [isStepCount(limits.rounds + 1), overBudget],  // 40 rounds of tools, or $3
  prepareStep,                                             // after the last round: tools off, so it must answer
});

```

That's the whole loop. The SDK calls the model, runs the tools it asks for, sends back the results, and repeats until the model answers without asking for a tool, or a limit stops it.

Run the agent the same way you ran the floor, then compare the two: 

```
# Terminal 1: the agent, with its three library tools (the default)
cd rag-agent/agent
npm start

# Terminal 2
cd rag-agent/harness
npm run eval -- --name agent --runs 3 --yes
open results/report.html

```

In the report, pick `agent`, then pick `floor` to compare. It shows the difference, the questions won, lost and tied, and which stamps changed. Ours, on 14 Nov:

| | The floor | The agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Score | 0.582 | 0.729 |
| Strict passes | 25 of 54 | 35 of 54 |
| Confidently wrong | 5 | 0 |
| Median cost and time an answer | $0.023, 59 s | $0.047, 36 s |

What's noise and how to deal with it?

Run the same agent several times with nothing changed, and see how far the score moves. Three runs of the first version of my main build (58 questions, 3 answers each):

| Run | Score |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.742 |
| 2 | 0.729 |
| 3 | 0.731 |

Nothing changed, yet the score moved by 0.013. Compared question by question, the differences between runs stretched from −0.039 to +0.027. So a change had to win by about 0.03 before I believed it.

...

- Data makes or breaks your agent. A source that's missing, out of date or badly split hurt more than any prompt tweak I tried. This guide assumes you already have a RAG pipeline; for anything bigger than the repo's three Acts in SQLite, build your own and swap `library.ts` for it.

...

The agent and the harness, with every file this part uses: github.com/yuvraj2112/rag-agent

signals.title: Huawei open-sources MACaQ quantizer for running AI models locally
signals.excerpt:
## What happened

Huawei has released MACaQ, a quantization tool it had been using internally, as an open-source project built for local inference, according to the project's page on GitHub. The toolkit shrinks AI models that handle text, images, video and audio so they can run with llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch. It is distributed under the Apache License 2.0.

According to the project page, MACaQ quantized a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes while using 32.5 GB of device memory. The page also says it delivers lower perplexity than the MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ methods, or matches their best Llama-3-8B results while taking about one eleventh of the quantization time. Output formats include 2-, 3- and 4-bit GGUF files as well as W4A4 checkpoints.

A companion tool, MACaQ-R, reworks the weight codes inside existing GGUF models to raise their quality and tailor them to particular workloads. The resulting files still run on an unmodified llama.cpp installation. Separately, W4A4 kernels have been submitted as pull requests to the CANN software stack, although running complete models requires integration with an Ascend inference runtime.

## Context

The project measures itself against the MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ methods. It also compares its output with previously published GGUF builds of Qwen3-4B, using file size and KL divergence relative to FP16. The team has published a research paper describing the method and has posted a MACaQ-R version of the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B mixture-of-experts model on Hugging Face.

November 17, 2026

Sarvam has opened Sarvam Token Factory to everyone. Sarvam Token Factory is an inference platform from Sarvam that serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Developers reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API. For India-based teams, this means low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

## TL;DR

- Size: 8 models listed at launch, including Sarvam 105B (105B total, 9B active, 128K context), GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B.
- Runs on: NVIDIA B200 clusters in India. Sarvam 105B now fits on 1 B200 per replica. On-premise deployment is offered to enterprises.
- Performance: Fastest first token from Mumbai on most tested cases, per Sarvam’s own measurements.
- Best: Kimi K3.1 Pro at 6,177 tokens/s per GPU vs 3,213 for InferenceX, at 70 tokens/s per user (1.9x).

## What is Sarvam Token Factory?

It is a managed inference stack, not a single model. Sarvam first previewed it as Sarvam Inference at its Epoch event. The launch post lists 8 models: Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B.

The docs split them into 2 groups. Pay-as-you-go models run on shared endpoints. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.8 27B, Clef and EmbeddingGemma 2 need Provisioned Throughput, enabled per organisation.

## How does it work?

The stack has 3 layers around a shared cache:

- Control plane: a cache-aware router, admission control and a planner.
- Inference engine: separate GPU pools for prefill and decode.
- Cache: GPU memory plus a shared G3 store built on Mooncake.

It builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, and an engineer approves each deployment.

Caching drives most of the gains. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves 450B+ tokens per day, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. On GLM 5.3, the planner cut prefill GPU-hours from 32.3 to 17.1 under the same replayed load.

For Sarvam 105B, MXFP8 weights plus speculative decoding raised output throughput about 2.2x. That cut each replica from 2 B200s to 1. Sarvam says none of these changes reduced accuracy.

## How fast is it? Benchmarks

All numbers below come from Sarvam’s launch post. They are self-reported.

- Sarvam 105B: 0.2 s first token and 330 tokens/s for a single user.
- Gemma 4 31B (10K prompt, Mumbai): 0.40 s first token and 308 tokens/s, vs 2.00 s and 193 tokens/s at the only other provider.
- Kimi K3.1 Pro (16 B200s): 6,177 vs 3,213 tokens/s per GPU against InferenceX at 70 tokens/s per user.
- Heavy agent load (72 sessions): median first token 0.8 s vs 11.6 s for InferenceX.
- GLM 5.3 Flash (64 sessions): p99 first token 3.2 s vs 14.1 s for stock vLLM and Dynamo.

The results are not a clean sweep. On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a 10K prompt, Together posts 0.71 s first token vs Sarvam’s 0.90 s. Together also streams faster, at 278 tokens/s vs 130 on Sarvam Standard.

## Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference

NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions.

### Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance

Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode.

| Prefill and decode optimization | Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. |
| Model-specific GPU execution | Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. |
| Speculative generation and verification | Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. |

signals.title: OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
signals.excerpt:
Sasha Blumenfeld · 11/16/2026

We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond. Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face. Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.

The integration also runs the other way. OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them. The setup guide has the steps.

## What you get on Hugging Face

Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider. OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability. You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.

You also get automatic failover. If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers. If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.

When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request. Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.

You stay in control of the trade-off. Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as `:fastest`, `:cheapest`, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API. A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.

Each model page has a new Providers tab with live price, speed, and uptime for every provider. You can see your spend by provider and turn off any provider you don’t want to use.

160 models from 38 labs are available this way today, which is every model OpenRouter serves that has a page on the Hub. They include the open-weight models developers use most on OpenRouter, where open-weight models carried about 70% of paid tokens in October:

- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
- MoonshotAI Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3
- Z.ai GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash
- Qwen3.8 27B
- MiniMax M3.1 Flash

signals.title: LongCat-2.5: Meituan open-sources a 1.6T agent model under MIT, trained and served without Nvidia · Harel Asaf
signals.excerpt:
Meituan's LongCat team released the weights for LongCat-2.5 this week under the MIT license, and the combination matters: a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with roughly 48B active parameters per token, native multimodality, a 512K-token context window, and agentic-coding benchmarks in Claude Opus 5 territory, trained and deployed without any Nvidia hardware. The weights landed on Hugging Face about a week after the model's official unveiling, alongside a quantized W4A4 variant and an NPU deployment recipe. This is now one of the strongest truly open models you can actually download, modify, and serve yourself, with the caveat that serving it takes a small data center. All benchmark and infrastructure numbers below come from the model card and are vendor-reported.

...

## The benchmarks, all vendor-reported

The model card's table compares LongCat-2.5 against LongCat-2.0 and frontier models including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Numbers marked with an asterisk on the card are cited from external sources rather than run by the team, so treat cross-vendor comparisons with the usual care.

The highlights: Terminal-Bench v2.1 at 88.4, just under Opus 5's 89.1 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's 90.6, and far above LongCat-2.0's 70.8. On the harder Terminal-Bench v4.0 the gap to Opus 5 widens, 38.5 to 53.9, and on Program Bench (Almost Resolved) it scores 25.5 against Opus 5's 37.0. PaperBench is a bright spot at 82.1, near the top of the table, and 3DCodeBench at 55.4 is the highest score listed. Against its own predecessor the jump is dramatic across the board: DeepSWE goes from 9.7 to 64.6, AutomationBench from 15.8 to 51.8, JobBench from 44.4 to 65.4.

The honest reading: this is a frontier-adjacent agent model that trades blows with the best on some evaluations and clearly trails Opus 5 on terminal-heavy work. For an open-weights model under MIT, that is a new watermark.

## Trained and served without Nvidia

The infrastructure section of the card is as interesting as the benchmarks. Training ran on domestic Chinese AI accelerators, and the team reports supernode-aware parallelism, sharding, and communication-computation overlap delivering 86% higher per-device throughput than a DDP baseline on long-sequence SFT tasks. The RL infrastructure keeps token log probabilities bitwise-identical across training, prefill, and decoding, which anyone who has debugged train-serve skew will appreciate, and KV cache work nearly doubled decode KV capacity without increasing TPOT on the tested workload.

The W4A4 quantization story is the deployment enabler: expert weights and activations go to native INT4 on domestic accelerators using FlatQuant-style learnable transformations, with accuracy the team says is comparable to the unquantized model on evaluated benchmarks. Against a W8A8 MoE baseline, online stress tests show 43.3% higher prefill throughput, 42.77% higher decode throughput, 15.91% lower TTFT, and 19.72% lower TPOT, with grouped GEMM kernels averaging 1.73x speedup. Combined with KV cache quantization, W4A4KV8 delivers 92% higher decode throughput than W8A8KV16. A separate W4A4 weight release is published alongside the main model.

## How to actually run it

Be realistic about the hardware. The reference NPU deployment, documented in the SGLang-FluentLLM repository, targets Huawei's Ascend Atlas A2 platform, and the sample configuration is a 194-card Atlas A2 Pod cluster with 16 cards per prefill/decode machine and 2 cards for the encoder. At 1.6T parameters even INT4 weights are in the hundreds of gigabytes, so this is a cluster model, not a laptop model. The deployment stack is CANN 9.0.0 with torch_npu and torchair matched to PyTorch 2.9.0, which tells you the software path is Huawei-first.

If you do not run Ascend hardware, the practical routes are the hosted API on the official LongCat platform, which sits behind a Meituan account login so I could not verify pricing without signing up, or waiting for community inference support. GPU-oriented serving stacks have not published verified LongCat-2.5 recipes at the time of writing, and I would not assume vLLM or stock SGLang handles the architecture without checking.

...

Vendor tables with asterisked competitor numbers are not independent evaluations, and several strong results here are self-run only. Do not assume the model is cheap to serve because it is efficient on Ascend: the reference deployment is a 194-card pod, and nothing about the release suggests single-node practicality. And the MIT license covers the weights, not the compute you would need to use them.

signals.excerpt:
## See: your agents and their token path, model spend

Start with what’s running. Nasiko’s agent auto scan discovers coding agents running across your teams and shows which are active. Open any run to follow what happened: its model calls, the agents it handed work to, and the tools it used.

Model spend lands in one cost schema across vendors, broken out by team, model, agent, and harness, instead of scattered across separate provider dashboards. The history builds as you go, so next quarter’s plan starts from real spend by team and agent instead of a guess.

...

## Cut: reduce token waste

Cheaper tokens help, but they don’t fix how a run uses them. Increasingly, agents resend the same background, carry context they no longer need, and default to models bigger than the job requires. Nasiko gives you a lever for each:

- Context selection and compression removes what the model doesn’t need before the call is sent.
- Caching stores repeated context so agents don’t pay to resend it, and recommends what's worth caching.
- Model selection per agent puts each agent on the model its work calls for, set once, centrally, across providers.

A research agent that resends the same background document on every call is a caching candidate. An agent drafting routine replies may not need the largest model available. Together, these levers help keep model spend from growing in step with adoption.

signals.title: llama.cpp FP8 has landed, but only per-tensor FP8 checkpoints stay FP8: we checked 13 of them — sysnote
signals.excerpt:
llama.cpp can now keep FP8 weights as FP8. Three pull requests by NVIDIA's Oliver Simons (ORippler) landed in the last three weeks: #27512 added an OCP FP8 E4M3 tensor type and taught the converter to keep FP8 tensors instead of dequantizing them (merged October 29), #28392 added FP8 KV caches (`-ctk f8_e4m3 -ctv f8_e4m3`, merged November 10), and #28413 added CUDA kernels that run FP8 matrix multiplies on FP8 tensor cores (merged November 11). All three are in llama.cpp v1.0.0, tagged on November 13. The release notes list the KV cache; the CUDA kernels are in the ggml v1.0.0 notes.

That sounds like "FP8 checkpoints from Hugging Face now just work". They mostly don't, yet, and the reason is in the converter: it keeps FP8 only when a tensor has a single scale. We checked how 13 public FP8 checkpoints store their scales. Seven would stay FP8. The other six, including Qwen's and DeepSeek's official FP8 releases, are still dequantized to 16-bit, as before.

## Which checkpoints stay FP8

An FP8 E4M3 number has a 3-bit mantissa and tops out at 448, so FP8 checkpoints ship scale factors next to the weights. Their layout varies: one scale for the whole tensor, one per output row ("channel"), or one per 128×128 block. In `conversion/base.py`, the new `_prepare_fp8_e4m3_tensors` keeps a weight as `F8_E4M3` only if its scale has exactly one element (`prod(scale.shape) == 1`). Everything else goes through the old `dequant_fp8` path. FP8 is also kept only with the default `--outtype auto`; `--fp8-as-q8` still turns FP8 weights into Q8_0.

We read the `config.json` and the safetensors header of the first shard of each checkpoint and matched the scale shapes against that rule. We didn't run the conversion, so this is a reading of the code rather than a test:

| Checkpoint | FP8 weight scales | After `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nvidia/Qwen3-8B-FP8` (ModelOpt) | per tensor, plus `k_scale`/`v_scale` | stays FP8 |
| `nvidia/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8` | per tensor, plus `k_scale`/`v_scale` | stays FP8 |
| `nvidia/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B-NVFP4` (FP8 layers) | per tensor, plus `k_scale`/`v_scale` | stays FP8 |
| `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (FP8 layers) | per tensor | stays FP8 |
| `RedHatAI/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8` | per tensor | stays FP8 |
| `RedHatAI/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-FP8` | per tensor | stays FP8 |
| `mistralai/Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512` | per tensor (`weight_scale_inv`) | stays FP8 |
| `RedHatAI/Qwen3.5-4B-FP8-dynamic` | per channel | dequantized |
| `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (FP8 layers) | per channel | dequantized |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8` | 128×128 blocks | dequantized |
| `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8` | 128×128 blocks | dequantized |
| `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2` | 128×128 blocks | dequantized |
| `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2` | 128×128 blocks | dequantized |

The pattern is the producer. NVIDIA's ModelOpt and the older static Red Hat recipes use per-tensor scales, while the official FP8 releases of Chinese labs use DeepSeek's 128×128 blocks.

...

## What runs where

FP8 weights now work on every CUDA GPU, but they only run as FP8 math on some. From `ggml-cuda/fp8.cu`:

- Prefill and other large batches go through cuBLASLt FP8 GEMM, but only when `fp8_mma_hardware_available()` is true: NVIDIA compute capability from Ada Lovelace (8.9) up to, but not including, Rubin. That covers RTX 40 and 50, L40S, H100 and B200. Activations are quantized to FP8 on the fly with one scale for the whole activation tensor, its absolute maximum divided by 448.
- Small batches (eight tokens or fewer, which covers single-user decoding) use the MMVF kernel. It converts FP8 weights to floating point and multiplies in F32. Token generation reads half the bytes of BF16, but doesn't use FP8 math.
- Older GPUs fall back to cuBLAS with the weights converted to FP16, so an RTX 3090 loads these files and runs them like a 16-bit model.
- Elsewhere, the CPU has a scalar reference implementation. Metal explicitly reports FP8 matrix multiplies and row lookups as unsupported, so on a Mac those operations fall back to the CPU. Vulkan support is a separate draft, #29791 by Ruben Ortlam (0cc4m). The PR also defers dedicated FP8 MoE kernels, on the reasoning that "folks tend to quantize those layers to 4/2-bit".

Simons's own numbers are for the FP8 layers of `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` on an RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell. With those layers kept in FP8 (19.56 GiB file), `llama-bench` measured 3,582 tokens/s on an 8,196-token prompt. With the same layers as Q8_0 (19.98 GiB), it measured 3,063 tokens/s. That makes prefill 17% faster, while generation was flat at about 40 tokens/s either way. Wikitext-2 perplexity was 5.4527 with FP8 layers and 5.4727 with Q8_0 layers, both with a BF16 KV cache. These come from one GPU, one model and the author's own early build, measured on just 10 chunks. They suggest more than they prove.

## The FP8 KV cache is barely smaller than Q8_0

`-ctk f8_e4m3 -ctv f8_e4m3` stores each cached key and value in one byte. llama.cpp's existing Q8_0 cache uses 34 bytes per 32 values, one FP16 scale plus 32 int8s, or 1.06 bytes per value. The FP8 cache saves about 6% of KV memory compared with `q8_0`, and half compared with F16. In the same perplexity table it was a little worse than Q8_0: 5.4550 against 5.4491, with BF16 at 5.4527.

So for an ordinary GGUF model, `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` is still as good a choice.
